newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress sees crisis over in a week.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress sees crisis over in a week.

text.p: India's Congress party said on Monday the nation's political crisis could be over in a week as the ousted United Front alliance stepped up efforts to find a successor to caretaker Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda.
Deve Gowda broke a political logjam on Sunday when he told his 15-party coalition that he would meet Congress's demand and step down if his partners so decided.
Until Sunday, Deve Gowda and his partners had steadfastly refused to bow to Congress's stipulation that the coalition change leaders before a new government could be formed.

"We have to keep the national interest above everything else," said United Front leader Chandrababu Naidu, considered a leading contender to succeed Deve Gowda as prime minister. "Why should the nation pay for our rigid stands?... The institution is important, not individuals."

Deve Gowda's reversal opened the door to a possible new alignment, with Congress supporting a fresh governing coalition led by the United Front and strongly resembling the centre-left team that fell last week.
It also dramatically reduced the prospects -- at least for now -- of mid-term polls that could benefit Hindu nationalists.
Congress, which provoked Deve Gowda's downfall last Friday by withdrawing its needed support for his 10-month-old government, welcomed the caretaker prime minister's move.
"If they have any other leader, we are prepared to support them," Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil said.
Asked how long it would take the United Front and Congress to work out a new deal, Gadgil said: "About a week."

The United Front was to meet on Thursday to choose a new chief. Apart from Andhra Pradesh chief minister Naidu, who said he was not interested, leading contenders included regional Tamil leader G.K. Moopanar, Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral and Industry Minister Murasoli Maran.

The policy-making Congress Working Committee was set to meet in New Delhi at 7 p.m. (1330 GMT) on Monday. Newspapers said it was shaping up as a battle between Congress president Sitaram Kesri and the party's leader in the lower house, Sharad Pawar, who has given lukewarm support to the move to topple Deve Gowda.

Gadgil said Kesri would have no trouble satisfying a United Front demand that he withdraw a letter to President Shankar Dayal Sharma revoking Congress support for the United Front and staking a claim to power.
While the United Front said it was open to forming a fresh coalition under a new leader, it expressed concern over the "credibility" and "durability" of Congress' support.
"That is a matter of negotiation," Gadgil said.
The right-wing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) scoffed at its rivals' efforts to forge a new government.
"I think they are going to have another experiment," BJP spokeswoman Sushma Swaraj told Reuters. "If the first arrangement was a zero, this will also prove to be a zero."
Swaraj predicted that the new United Front-led government would last only six months because, like Deve Gowda's coalition, it would fall victim to differences with Congress.
The BJP is parliament's biggest party with 162 seats in the 542-member lower house. With its allies it controls 193 votes, ahead of the United Front's 178 and Congress's 140.
Opinion surveys show the BJP would likely be strengthened if the second general elections in a year were held now.

BJP leader Atal Bihari Vajpayee said the president should not ask the same coalition that lost a confidence vote to form another government. "It would be better to have another parliamentary election," he told reporters in Lucknow city.
